summary:
FLAMMA is an AI-powered web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into clear fire-safety answers for human space exploration. We cleaned eight NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations (Saffire-II, BASS, BASS-II, ACME CFI-G, ACME BRE, SAME-R, SPICE and FLEX) into one shared format, organized by NASA's three fire-safety pillars: prevention, detection and suppression.

Users can set a scenario in "Will It Burn?" (ISS cabin, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars base or spacesuit air) and see the closest real NASA tests, ranked and summarized. Each investigation has its own page with graphs of its results, the cleaned table beside NASA's original, and CSV downloads for modeling. "Ask" answers questions in plain English using Gemini with retrieval from NASA documents, and cites its sources.

This matters because future Moon bases will use more oxygen at lower pressure, where materials burn more easily, yet the data is hard to find, compare and interpret. FLAMMA makes it searchable and explainable for students, researchers and engineers. It also shows how space fire research protects people on Earth, from firefighter gear to smoke detectors, with a Malaysian perspective and a Malay language option.

All required documents  (30s Demo, 3 mins video, Project pdf etc) are submitted on https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1_GcmemDiMWEr8O96pNN-LlfqHTw1boIi

Notes: Logo of FLAMMA is drawn by me.
details:
What FLAMMA does

FLAMMA is an AI-powered web dashboard that makes NASA's microgravity fire-safety research easy to find, compare and understand. It brings together eight investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database: Saffire-II, BASS, BASS-II, ACME CFI-G, ACME BRE, SAME-R, SPICE and FLEX. It organizes them by NASA's three fire-safety pillars: prevention, detection and suppression.

  • Will It Burn?: users pick a scenario (ISS cabin, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars base, spacesuit or Earth room) or set the oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity and fuel themselves. FLAMMA ranks the closest real NASA tests, shows what happened in them, gives an AI summary, and plots where NASA's data has tests and where there are gaps.
  • Ask: users ask questions in plain English. Gemini answers using retrieval from NASA documents (the Researcher's Guide to Combustion Science, the FLEX results report, NASA Spinoff articles, the Apollo and Mir histories, and lunar flammability research) and cites each source.
  • Investigation pages: each investigation has its own page with its objective and hypothesis, graphs of its results with plain-language takeaways calculated from the data, and the cleaned table beside NASA's original table. Users can download every table as a CSV for modeling. Ask and Summarize on this page answer about that investigation only.
  • Compare: investigations side by side by hardware, fuel, oxygen, pressure, airflow and outcomes, also downloadable.
  • Back on Earth: how space fire research led to firefighter air tanks, smoke detectors, fire-resistant clothing and fine-water-mist extinguishers.

How it works

A Python script cleans NASA's raw PSI tables into one shared format: common column names, converted units, outcomes read from NASA's wording, and fixed typos such as wrong dates. NASA's raw files are never changed. The website is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with hand-made SVG graphs. Two serverless functions on Vercel call Google Gemini, so the API key never reaches the browser. NASA and JAXA documents are split into about 450 passages, and a BM25 search finds the best ones for each question. Gemini answers only from those passages and the NASA data.

Benefits and impact

Future Moon bases and rovers are expected to use more oxygen at lower pressure (30% or more at 10.2 psi), where materials burn more easily, and there is no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI yet. FLAMMA helps students, researchers and engineers quickly see which NASA tests are closest to these conditions, what happened, and where the gaps are. Researchers can download cleaned data for modeling and check it against NASA's original tables. FLAMMA also shows the public, including in Malaysia, how space fire research protects people on Earth.

Tools used

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python (pandas, pypdf), Node.js serverless functions, Google Gemini API, BM25 retrieval, Vercel, Git and GitHub, Google Translate, and an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). Data and images: NASA PSI, NASA technical documents and Spinoff, images.nasa.gov, and JAXA (courtesy).

What makes it creative

  • Users test a "what if" scenario instead of searching tables.
  • Every graph comes with a plain-language sentence calculated from the data, not written by hand.
  • Cleaned and original NASA tables sit side by side, so anyone can check the data cleaning.
  • History tells the story: Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir and Artemis II lead into the science.
  • A local link: Malaysia's first astronaut, Malaysian fire statistics, and a Bahasa Melayu option.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: the AI must cite sources, must not invent causes or numbers, and must say when the data doesn't cover a question. Data gaps, such as no Moon or Mars gravity data, are shown openly.
  • Transparency: original data is kept next to the cleaned version, and every source is cited.
  • Copyright: images and documents are credited. JAXA documents are used with credit and kept out of the public code.
  • Security: the API key stays on the server.
  • Accessibility: colorblind-checked chart colors, light and dark mode, readable on phones, and text descriptions for images.
  • Free-tier limits: the site keeps working, showing NASA data, even if the AI is unavailable.
